title: Pivot Tables
summary: Build a PivotTable to summarise Orders data by city and status, then change the value-field summary function.

steps.title: What a PivotTable Does and How to Build One
steps.lede: A PivotTable summarises your Orders data by city, status, or any other field — no formulas required.

blocks.text: Reading down a long Orders sheet to compare total amounts by city and status by hand would take forever. A PivotTable is a tool to calculate, summarize, and analyze data that lets you see comparisons, patterns, and trends in your data.

To create a PivotTable, select the data cells, select Insert > PivotTable, choose where to place the PivotTable report, and select OK. To add a field, select its checkbox in the PivotTable Fields pane; non-numeric fields go to Rows and numeric fields go to Values by default. A field can be moved to a different area by dragging it there.

Filters area fields appear as top-level report filters above the PivotTable. Columns area fields appear as Column Labels at the top. Rows area fields appear as Row Labels on the left. Values area fields appear as summarised numeric values in the body. Building a PivotTable from your Orders data with City in Rows, Status in Columns, and Amount in Values gives a grid of summarised order amounts for every city/status combination.

steps.title: What Each PivotTable Area Displays
steps.lede: Each of the four drop zones produces a distinct visual output in the PivotTable.

blocks.text: Filters area fields are shown as top-level report filters above the PivotTable. Columns area fields are shown as Column Labels at the top of the PivotTable. Rows area fields are shown as Row Labels on the left side of the PivotTable. Values area fields are shown as summarised numeric values in the body of the PivotTable.

steps.title: Creating a PivotTable and Reading Its Areas
steps.lede: Test your understanding of the creation steps and what each area displays.

public.prompt: You drag the city field into the Rows area of a PivotTable. Where does city appear in the finished PivotTable?

options.text: As Row Labels on the left side of the PivotTable, with one row per city.
As Column Labels across the top of the PivotTable, with one column per city.
As a top-level report filter above the PivotTable.
As summarized numeric values in the body of the PivotTable.

opt_b.message: Column Labels appear when a field is placed in the Columns area, not the Rows area. A field in the Rows area appears as Row Labels on the left side.

opt_c.message: A top-level report filter appears when a field is placed in the Filters area. A field in the Rows area appears as Row Labels on the left side of the PivotTable.

opt_d.message: Summarized numeric values appear in the Values area. A field in the Rows area appears as Row Labels — one row per unique value of that field.

correct.message: Correct! A field placed in the Rows area appears as Row Labels on the left side of the PivotTable — one row for each unique value of that field (e.g., one row per city).

incorrect.message: The Rows area produces Row Labels on the left side of the PivotTable. Each unique value of the field (e.g., each city name) gets its own row.

hints: Think about the four areas: Filters (top), Columns (top header), Rows (left side), Values (body numbers).
The Rows area places field values down the left side of the PivotTable as row labels.

steps.title: Building a PivotTable to Answer a Question
steps.lede: Apply your knowledge of fields, areas, and creation steps to a summarisation task.

public.prompt: You want a PivotTable that shows the total order amount for each city, with cities listed down the left and a single column of totals. Which field placement achieves this?

options.text: city in Rows area; amount in Values area.
city in Columns area; amount in Values area.
city in Values area; amount in Rows area.
city in Filters area; amount in Rows area.

opt_b.message: Placing city in the Columns area would spread city names across the top as column headers, not down the left as row labels. To list cities down the left, place city in the Rows area.

opt_c.message: The Values area holds numeric summaries, not category labels. city is a text field and should go in the Rows area; amount is numeric and should go in the Values area.

opt_d.message: The Filters area creates a top-level report filter, not row labels. To list cities down the left side, place city in the Rows area.

correct.message: Correct! city in the Rows area creates one row per city on the left side; amount in the Values area fills in the total for each city. That gives you the city-by-total layout you need.

incorrect.message: To list cities down the left with totals beside them, place city in the Rows area and amount in the Values area. Rows area → left-side labels; Values area → numeric summaries.

hints: Rows area = left-side labels (one row per unique value). Values area = numeric summaries in the body.
Match the field type to the area: text/category fields go in Rows or Columns; numeric fields go in Values.

steps.title: Build a PivotTable from the Orders Data
steps.lede: Create a PivotTable and place fields in the Rows, Columns, and Values areas.

public.prompt: A PivotTable with city in the Rows area and amount in the Values area would show the total amount for each city. In cell F1, write a formula that returns the total amount for Lagos orders — the value that would appear in the Lagos row of that PivotTable. Use SUMIF with the city range B2:B21, the criterion "Lagos", and the amount range D2:D21. (Note: SUMIF was covered in the earlier Text, Date, and Conditional Aggregation lesson.)

correct.message: Correct! =SUMIF(B2:B21,"Lagos",D2:D21) returns 28000 — the total amount for Lagos orders. In a PivotTable with city in Rows and amount in Values, this is exactly the value that would appear in the Lagos row.

incorrect.message: Use SUMIF with three arguments: the city range (B2:B21), the criterion ("Lagos"), and the amount range (D2:D21). The formula is =SUMIF(B2:B21,"Lagos",D2:D21).

hints: SUMIF takes three arguments: =SUMIF(range, criteria, sum_range). The range is the city column, the criteria is "Lagos", and the sum_range is the amount column.
Make sure to put Lagos in double quotes inside the formula: =SUMIF(B2:B21,"Lagos",D2:D21).

steps.title: Changing How Values Are Summarised
steps.lede: The Values area defaults to Sum for numbers and Count for text — and you can change it.

blocks.text: Data in a PivotTable's Values area summarises the underlying source data by default using the SUM function for numeric values and the COUNT function for text values. Placing Amount in Values on your Orders PivotTable defaults to a total of every matching order's amount, not an average.

To change a value field's summary function, select the field in the Values area, then on the PivotTable Analyze tab select Active Field > Field Settings (or right-click the value and choose Value Field Settings), select the Summarize Values By tab, and choose the function you want, such as Average. Switching Amount from Sum to Average turns the same PivotTable from showing total revenue per city into showing average order value per city.

steps.title: Changing a PivotTable's Value-Field Summary Function
steps.lede: See how to open Value Field Settings and switch between Sum and Average.

segments.label: Opening Value Field Settings to switch a summary function from Sum to Average
segments.summary: Starting from a PivotTable that already has a numeric field in the Values area, the presenter opens Value Field Settings two ways: first by clicking the field's dropdown arrow in the Values area and selecting Value Field Settings, then by right-clicking the value cell in the PivotTable itself. In both cases the same dialog appears; selecting Average and clicking OK immediately updates the displayed numbers, and the process is reversed by returning to the dialog and selecting Sum.

segments.label: Why a PivotTable value field defaults to Count for text and Sum for numbers
segments.summary: A PivotTable's Values area automatically chooses its calculation type based on the data type of the field: text fields default to Count because text cannot be summed, while numeric fields default to Sum. A numeric column that contains blank cells is treated as mixed and also defaults to Count; the same applies to columns containing error values such as #REF! or #N/A.

steps.title: Default Summarisation by Data Type
steps.lede: Test your understanding of when a PivotTable defaults to Sum versus Count.

public.prompt: You add the status field (which contains text values: Delivered, Pending, Cancelled) to the Values area of a PivotTable. What summary function does Excel apply by default?

options.text: COUNT — because the field contains text values, not numbers.
SUM — because SUM is always the default for any field in the Values area.
AVERAGE — because Excel averages all values by default.
MAX — because Excel picks the largest value by default.

opt_b.message: SUM is the default only for numeric fields. When the field contains text values, Excel defaults to COUNT instead, because you cannot add text values together.

opt_c.message: AVERAGE is not the default for any field type. Excel defaults to SUM for numeric fields and COUNT for text fields.

opt_d.message: MAX is not the default. Excel defaults to SUM for numeric fields and COUNT for text fields.

correct.message: Correct! Excel defaults to COUNT for text fields in the Values area, because text values cannot be summed. For numeric fields it defaults to SUM.

incorrect.message: Excel uses COUNT as the default for text fields in the Values area (you cannot sum text), and SUM as the default for numeric fields.

hints: Ask yourself: can you add text values like 'Delivered' and 'Pending' together? If not, what would Excel do instead?
The rule is: numeric field → SUM by default; text field → COUNT by default.

steps.title: Switch the Summary Function to Average
steps.lede: Change the Values area from Sum to Average using Value Field Settings.

public.prompt: A PivotTable currently shows the Sum of amount for each city. You want to change the Values area to show the Average of amount instead. In cell F1, write a formula that returns the average order amount across all 20 orders — the overall average that the PivotTable grand total row would show after switching to Average. Use AVERAGE with the range D2:D21.

correct.message: Correct! =AVERAGE(D2:D21) returns 4955 — the average order amount. After changing the PivotTable's Values field setting from Sum to Average, the grand total row would show this value.

incorrect.message: Use AVERAGE with the amount range: =AVERAGE(D2:D21). This returns the average order amount across all 20 orders.

hints: The AVERAGE function takes a range as its argument: =AVERAGE(D2:D21).
The amount column is column D, rows 2 through 21 (20 orders).

steps.title: Pivot Tables — Key Points
steps.lede: You can now build a PivotTable, place fields in the four areas, and change the summary function.

blocks.text: A PivotTable lets you calculate, summarise, and analyse data to see comparisons, patterns, and trends. Select the data, choose Insert > PivotTable, and drag fields into Rows, Columns, Values, or Filters. Non-numeric fields default to Rows; numeric fields default to Values. The Values area defaults to Sum for numbers and Count for text. To change the summary function, open Value Field Settings and choose from the Summarize Values By tab.

remediation_steps.title: Creating a PivotTable Step by Step
remediation_steps.lede: Walk through the creation steps and see what each area produces.

blocks.text: To create a PivotTable: select the data cells, choose Insert > PivotTable, pick where to place the report, and click OK. In the Fields pane, check City — it goes to Rows because it is text. Check Amount — it goes to Values because it is numeric. Drag Status to Columns. The result: Row Labels show cities on the left, Column Labels show statuses at the top, and the body shows summarised amounts. Filters area fields would appear above the table as top-level report filters.

remediation_steps.title: Choosing Fields and Areas for a Summarisation Task
remediation_steps.lede: Match the question you want to answer to the correct field placement.

blocks.text: To answer 'What is the total order amount per city?' place City in Rows and Amount in Values — the PivotTable sums Amount for each city. To add a breakdown by status, drag Status to Columns. To filter to a single city, drag City to Filters instead of Rows. Non-numeric fields added to the Fields pane go to Rows by default; numeric fields go to Values. You can always drag a field from one area to another.

remediation_steps.title: Sum vs. Count: The Default Rule
remediation_steps.lede: The data type of the field determines which summary function the PivotTable uses by default.

blocks.text: When you drag a numeric field such as Amount into the Values area, the PivotTable defaults to Sum — it adds up all matching values. When you drag a text field such as Status into Values, the PivotTable defaults to Count — it counts how many rows match. You can always change the function via Value Field Settings.
